The abbreviation B.C.E. (Before Common Era) and negative years are general conventions used to represent eras that precede the earliest recorded dates in our calendars.

Prerequisites

The study of genealogy requires basic knowledge of mathematics, literature, the languages in which the documents are written, history, and biology. We understand that many people do not have enough time to study all of these subjects in depth. To help you, we have gathered the following texts, which will serve as foundational resources for studying genealogy:

  • Origin: a general overview of the origin of our species, based both on scientific research and on various beliefs ().
  • Scientific method: an explanation of the scientific method, including an example you can perform at home ().
  • Understanding Texts: a section that teaches techniques for understanding texts and explores their relationship with mathematics ().
  • My Ancestors: a guide to help you obtain the necessary documentation and begin building your family tree ().
  • Sources: an explanation of the various sources used in research ().
  • Natural Limits: an introduction to the concept of limits, using examples from the human body and from liquids ().
  • Chronology: an introduction to the various archaeological periods currently in use ().
  • Genealogical Trees (Chapter 1): studying families only when documents are available reduces the possibility of understanding who we are and leads to countless misunderstandings, such as interpreting poetic texts as literal descriptions ().

We therefore recommend studying the first chapter of the Genealogical Trees section before continuing with the remaining chapters.

Some families may require additional information. Whenever that is the case, such details will be listed below.

Navigation

The family visualization page of History Tracers is organized into three main sections:

  • Patriarch/Matriarch list: this section presents a list of the patriarchs/matriarchs who named a family or resided in a particular region.
  • People organized by patriarch/matriarch's family: when readers click on a family name or a region in the first section, they are taken to a segment that introduces the first documented individual, together with their descendants and concise personal histories. Texts supported by primary sources appear in a normal font, while hypotheses that lack verifiable sources appear in italic. Each historical account is accompanied by its corresponding primary sources and references, which can be accessed with a simple click.
  • Primary sources and references: a common misconception among genealogy researchers is to assume that a person who authored a book strictly followed the scientific method when writing about their own family history, and that no further checking is needed. To avoid this misleading assumption, the page clearly separates primary sources, which unquestionably confirm that a person existed, from other references found in publications such as noble genealogies. Religious texts are placed in a separate, respectful section; however, if those texts were written during the lifetime of the people they mention, they can also be cited as primary sources.
